sourceNote: Selective DGT editorial notes for 1 Peter.

1:13: “Gird up the loins of your mind” is Peter’s concrete metaphor; DGT keeps the imagery rather than replacing it with an abstract paraphrase such as “prepare your minds.”
2:2: λογικόν can mean rational/spiritual and is related to λόγος. In this context DGT uses “spiritual milk,” while the metaphor continues the newborn-infant imagery.
2:18: οἰκέται refers to household servants. The verse addresses people in an ancient household-servant relationship; DGT does not broaden the noun to all modern employees.
3:18: The final contrast is literally “put to death in flesh, made alive in spirit.” Whether “spirit” refers to Christ’s spirit or a spiritual mode of life is interpretively debated; DGT keeps the compact Greek contrast.
3:19: “The spirits in prison” is one of the most debated expressions in the letter. DGT translates the clause directly without identifying the spirits or specifying when the proclamation occurred.
3:21: ἐπερώτημα can denote an appeal, request, or pledge. DGT uses “appeal to God for a good conscience,” while retaining Peter’s explicit statement that baptism saves through Jesus Christ’s resurrection.
4:6: “The dead” has been interpreted in several ways. DGT leaves the reference unexpanded and translates Peter’s contrast between judgment “in flesh” and life “in spirit” directly.
5:13: “She who is in Babylon” may refer to a church personified as a chosen woman; “Babylon” has often been understood as Rome, but DGT leaves Peter’s wording uninterpreted.
